title: Al-Musawwir, the Fashioner
hook: the Fashioner, who shapes every form
tomorrow: Amira snapped at Jordan again. how many sorries still count?

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Bari': the Maker, the Shaper out of naught, the middle step between the plan and the form. He brings forth. Now the third step.
screen: `HE BRINGS FORTH.` → `THE THIRD STEP: THE FORM.`

segments.voice: Portrait mode on a phone blurs everything behind a face so the face stands out. Faces are what people point cameras at. So yesterday's question is a real one. If al-Musawwir, the Fashioner, shapes every face, can a person paint one? Amira isn't the first to ask. Muslim scholars have argued it out, and the argument starts with the name itself.
screen: `THE FACE STANDS OUT.` → `HE SHAPES EVERY FACE.` → `CAN A PERSON PAINT ONE?`

segments.voice: Al-Musawwir is the Fashioner, the One who gives each thing its form. In Pickthall's words: "He it is Who fashioneth you in the wombs as pleaseth Him." And the forms differ on purpose: "the difference of your languages and colours" is named among His signs. One human family, many faces, one Fashioner. Now the two views. View one: don't make images of living beings. A hadith in Bukhari's collection warns image-makers of punishment on the Day of Resurrection, and when a painter told Ibn Abbas that pictures were his living, Ibn Abbas told him, in paraphrase: if you must, paint trees and things that have no soul. Their best case: forming living things belongs to al-Musawwir, and a person shouldn't play at rivaling it. Trees are still a whole world to paint. View two: other scholars read those warnings as aimed at images made for worship, or made to compete with Allah's creating, and they point to a report that Aisha played with dolls in the Prophet's house. Their best case: a picture made to remember or to teach is neither an idol nor a rival, and the warnings were about those. Both views agree on the center: every living form is His work, and no picture of a face is the face itself. That's the line to tell a friend tonight: the debate about painting faces is a debate about how much honor to give the Fashioner.
screen: `AL-MUSAWWIR: HE GIVES EACH THING FORM.` · `MANY FACES, ONE FASHIONER.` · `VIEW ONE: PAINT TREES, NOT SOULS.` · `VIEW TWO: THE WARNING IS ABOUT IDOLS.` · then, large: `SHAPED BY HIM.`

segments.voice: Hold up one hand and look at it for the whole sit: the lines across the palm, the creases at each knuckle, the curve of each nail. Turn it slowly, front and back. No one drew this from a sketch you could see; in the Qur'an's picture, it was fashioned as He pleased.
Al-Musawwir: the Fashioner, who shapes every form, from the lines of a palm to the color of a face. The third of the three making names.
Hold onto this: shaped by him, every face on every street. That's three making names in three days.

screen: `DAY 1487 COUNTS.` → `NAME 13 OF 99 · AL-MUSAWWIR.` → `TOMORROW: HOW MANY SORRIES STILL COUNT?`

howItsDone: Muslim scholars hold different views on drawing living beings: some avoid images with faces and keep to plants, patterns and calligraphy; others allow pictures made to teach or remember, never for worship.

fork.setup: your cousin says no faces in any picture, ever. you lean the other way. to be fair, what's her best case?

fork.reveal: her view rests on hadith warnings and Ibn Abbas's advice. the other view answers that the warnings target idols and rivalry. both honor al-Musawwir; neither is a dislike of art.

chat.meaning: Scholars hold more than one view on painting faces. Hearing Dadi out, and knowing a mural can honor the Fashioner without faces, keeps everyone in.
